items.stem: The empirical distribution function is defined by:
items.explanation: The EDF is the average of indicators that equal one when an observation is at most x.

items.stem: The empirical CDF is:
items.explanation: As x increases, the set of observations counted as ≤x can only grow, so the empirical CDF cannot decrease.

items.stem: If a value occurs m times in a sample of size n, the EDF jump at that value is:
items.explanation: The cumulative count increases by m at that value. Dividing by n gives a jump of m/n.

items.stem: For x at or above the sample maximum, Fₙ(x) equals:
items.explanation: All n observations are at most x, so the empirical cumulative proportion is n/n=1.

items.stem: For an iid sample, E[Fₙ(x)] equals:
items.explanation: The EDF is an average of n Bernoulli indicators with success probability F(x), so its expectation is F(x).

items.stem: The Glivenko–Cantelli theorem concerns:
options: Convergence of the sample mean only
Uniform convergence of Fₙ to F
items.explanation: The theorem states that the supremum distance between empirical and population CDFs converges to zero almost surely.

items.stem: The sample is 2, 3, 3, 4, 6. Find Fₙ(3).
items.explanation: Three of five observations are at most 3, so Fₙ(3)=3/5=0.6.

items.stem: A sample of size 10 has a value occurring three times. What is the jump at that value?
items.explanation: The jump equals multiplicity divided by sample size: 3/10=0.3.

items.stem: If F(x)=0.4 and n=10, Var[Fₙ(x)] equals:
items.explanation: Var=F(1−F)/n=0.4×0.6/10=0.024. The maximum possible variance at this n is 0.025.

items.stem: For n=12, the empirical 0.75-quantile index under the inverse-CDF convention is:
items.explanation: ceil(np)=ceil(0.75×12)=ceil(9)=9, so the quantile is the ninth order statistic.

items.stem: A sample of size 8 has five observations at or below x, two of which equal x. Find the jump at x.
items.explanation: The jump is the tie multiplicity divided by n: 2/8=0.25.

items.stem: Which statements about Fₙ are correct? A. It is nondecreasing. B. It is right-continuous. C. It reaches one at or above the sample maximum. D. It can decrease at a tied value.
items.explanation: A, B and C are correct. D is false: a tie creates a larger upward jump, never a decrease.
statements: It reaches one at or above the sample maximum.
It can decrease at a tied value.

A.why: True: increasing x cannot remove previously counted observations.

B.why: True: the value at a jump includes observations equal to x.

C.why: True: all sample observations are counted above the maximum.

items.stem: The pointwise variance of the EDF is:
items.explanation: At a fixed x, the EDF is a sample proportion of Bernoulli indicators, giving variance F(x){1−F(x)}/n.

items.stem: For 0<p≤1, the inverse-CDF empirical p-quantile is:
items.explanation: The inverse-CDF definition selects the first order statistic at which Fₙ reaches or exceeds p, giving index ceil(np).

items.stem: If F(x)=0.5 and n=20, the maximum possible pointwise variance of Fₙ(x) is:
items.explanation: F(1−F)/n=0.5×0.5/20=0.0125, the maximum because p(1−p) is largest at p=0.5.

items.stem: The EDF is especially useful in the one-sample KS test because KS uses:
options: The number of tied values only
The maximum difference between empirical and reference CDFs
items.explanation: The KS statistic is the supremum of the absolute difference between the empirical CDF and the specified reference CDF.

items.stem: Which statements about empirical-CDF convergence are correct? A. Glivenko–Cantelli is uniform in x. B. The supremum gap tends to zero almost surely. C. It states exact equality for every finite sample. D. It applies to iid sampling from F.
items.explanation: A, B and D are correct. C is false: convergence is asymptotic, not exact equality for a finite sample.
statements: Glivenko–Cantelli convergence is uniform in x.
The supremum gap tends to zero almost surely.
It states exact equality for every finite sample.
It applies to iid sampling from F.

A.why: True: the theorem controls the supremum over all x.

B.why: True: the uniform distance converges to zero almost surely.

C.why: False: finite-sample empirical and population CDFs generally differ.

D.why: True: the standard theorem is stated for iid observations.

items.stem: For x≤y, F(x)=0.3, F(y)=0.6 and n=10. Cov(Fₙ(x),Fₙ(y)) equals:
For an even sample size, the inverse-CDF empirical median may differ from the conventional sample median because:
options: The inverse-CDF convention selects the lower central order statistic, while some medians average the middle pair
The empirical CDF has no jumps
items.explanation: The inverse-CDF definition uses X_(ceil(n/2)); some sample median conventions average X_(n/2) and X_(n/2+1). State the convention.

items.stem: Why is Fₙ right-continuous at an observed value x?
options: Because the definition includes observations equal to x
items.explanation: The definition uses Xᵢ≤x, so the jump is included at x and the function takes the post-jump value there.
